result.summary: RECONSTRUCTED HANDOFF -- written 2026-09-03 after the fact from the run's real, on-disk evidence (the design doc's own §5.4 and §10 OQ-3, both of which today read as already-reworked/RESOLVED, carrying an explicit, dated account of exactly this FAIL and its fix). Timestamps are reconstructed approximations, not real clock reads. Two BLOCKER findings. BLOCKER 1: §10 OQ-3 (URL-freeze-on-retry) was left as an open question in the original draft despite a real, directly-applicable precedent already existing in this codebase -- Letflow.Webhooks.attempt_loop/7 (lib/letflow/webhooks.ex, confirmed at reconstruction time to start at line 266 and run through roughly line 313) freezes its target URL once at dispatch time and re-validates it fresh on every retry attempt, but never re-renders or re-resolves the URL template itself. The design's own draft failed to state this same discipline explicitly for service_task_dispatches' rendered_url, leaving open whether a retry would re-render the URL template against possibly-changed instance variables (a real correctness/security hazard: a URL that passed UrlValidator.validate/2 at first render could resolve differently on a later attempt if re-rendered against drifted variables). BLOCKER 2: the original claim-query design specified an invented, unverified locking clause -- lock("FOR UPDATE OF d0 SKIP LOCKED"), a binding-qualified lock hardcoding Ecto's auto-generated join-binding alias d0 as a literal string -- with zero codebase precedent. Independently grepped the real codebase for any FOR UPDATE OF-qualified lock (lib/letflow/repository.ex, engine.ex, definitions.ex, webhooks.ex, tasks.ex, scheduler.ex): zero matches. Every existing lock(...) call in this project is a bare lock("FOR UPDATE") or lock("FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED") on a query with no join -- including the design's own cited mirror, Letflow.Scheduler.claim_due_timer_ids/2 (lib/letflow/scheduler.ex, confirmed at reconstruction time to run roughly lines 222-234), whose query is a single-table SELECT with no join at all, so it never had a double-lock hazard to solve in the first place. The qualified-lock syntax was invented, not verified against a real precedent, and Postgres's own per-joined-table FOR UPDATE semantics (locking every joined table's matching rows unless explicitly restricted) make an unverified qualified-lock clause a real correctness risk if it had shipped as designed.

issues.description: OQ-3 (URL-freeze-on-retry) left open despite a real, directly-applicable precedent: Letflow.Webhooks.attempt_loop/7 (lib/letflow/webhooks.ex ~lines 266-313) freezes the target URL once and re-validates fresh on every retry, never re-rendering. Resolve OQ-3 by citing this precedent with real line numbers and stating the identical discipline for service_task_dispatches' rendered_url: rendered once at REQ-215's activation-time INSERT, dispatched against the frozen snapshot on every attempt including retries, re-validated via UrlValidator.validate/2 fresh on every attempt but never re-rendered.

The claim-query design specifies lock("FOR UPDATE OF d0 SKIP LOCKED"), an invented binding-qualified lock syntax with zero codebase precedent (grepped: no FOR UPDATE OF-qualified lock exists anywhere in lib/letflow/). Rewrite as a two-step select-then-lock: Step 1 an unlocked join query selecting eligible ids (joining instance_projections for the :active filter, no lock/1 call at all); Step 2 a single-table, bare lock("FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED") on service_task_dispatches only, re-selecting by the id list from Step 1 -- mirroring Letflow.Scheduler.claim_due_timer_ids/2's own bare-lock, no-join shape exactly.
